title: The VLT's Laser Guide Star
caption: The VLT's laser guide star and the southern Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: A laser beam from the Very Large Telescope's 8.2-meter Yepun telescope cuts across the southern sky, creating an artificial star at 90 km altitude in Earth's mesosphere. Behind it the Milky Way, seen edge-on, crosses the whole scene.

Several landmarks stand out along the Milky Way. Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, sits at the top, and the Carina Nebula appears as a bright patch beside the telescope. From the right edge toward the left run the Small Magellanic Cloud, which has the globular cluster 47 Tucanae beside it on the right, then the Large Magellanic Cloud and finally Canopus, the second brightest star in the sky.
The laser guide star is part of the VLT's adaptive optics system. It provides a reference point that lets the telescope correct its images for the blurring effect of the atmosphere.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way, the Carina Nebula and the Magellanic Clouds appear brighter than they would to an observer.

explore: A globular cluster such as 47 Tucanae is a dense ball of old stars. The photograph was taken by Gerhard Hüdepohl, who captured the laser, the telescope and these southern sky landmarks together.
alt: A laser beam from a telescope crosses a starry sky, with the Milky Way, a bright nebula near the telescope and two fuzzy dwarf galaxies.
